In multi-party democracies, you have an election and then the parties sort out who forms a government afterwards. So let's say a major party gets the biggest share, 35%. A smaller party has 10%. The smaller party will be invited to help form a government....but they won't be able to enact all of their agenda. Anything that the major party and the smaller party conflict on, the major party will usually win. So you can vote for something and then not get it. And then a centrist party would have to weigh in as well. And then all of that has to be balanced against what the other members of the coalition would have to say as well. You don't find out what that government would look like until well after the election.

In the American system, factions of movements fight for control of one of the two major parties in the primary, and only *then* does the race narrow to the binary choice in the general. Most of what having a multi-party democracy does is reverse the order of this process, meaning voters have arguably *even less* say in policy.
